Identification depth and digestion

Source: vignettes/digestion.Rmd
digestion.Rmd

The more digested a prey item, the coarser the rank it can be named to. That matters because digestion is not even across prey. Soft-bodied prey lose their identifying features faster than fish with otoliths or crustaceans with hard parts, so the material that can still be identified to species is a biased sample of what was eaten. Buckland et al. (2017) asked diet studies to report how prey condition affected identification. dv_digestion_diagnostic() gives you that table.

The data are the public ICES stomach-content extract that ships with the package (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see ?ices_diet), prepared as in the getting-started vignette.

library(DietView)

# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]

spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)

A caveat on the stages

ICES records digestion as a code, 0, 1 or 2. The labels used here (“0 pristine”, “1 affected”, “2 skeletal remains”) are inferred from the older ICES format, whose three classes match the shares of these codes; they are not taken from the ICES vocabulary. Read the stages as an ordered scale from fresh to digested and check the labels against the ICES documentation before you quote them. Records whose stage was not reported are kept as “not recorded”.

What the diagnostic computes

For every record, DietView finds the deepest rank with a name: its finest resolved rank. Records with no name at any rank are “Unresolved”. Within each digestion stage it then reports the share of records, and of weight, at each finest rank.

diag <- dv_digestion_diagnostic(prep)
head(diag[, c("digestion", "finest_rank", "n_records", "p_records", "p_weight")], 7)
#>    digestion finest_rank n_records p_records   p_weight
#> 1 0 pristine      Phylum        42  7.486631  3.1594482
#> 2 0 pristine       Class        26  4.634581  0.2300241
#> 3 0 pristine       Order       110 19.607843  2.2952781
#> 4 0 pristine      Family        82 14.616756  9.2883107
#> 5 0 pristine       Genus        16  2.852050  0.8581803
#> 6 0 pristine     Species       219 39.037433 82.5783551
#> 7 0 pristine  Unresolved        66 11.764706  1.5904035

Side by side, the record shares are easier to read:

round(xtabs(p_records ~ finest_rank + digestion, data = diag), 1)
#>             digestion
#> finest_rank  0 pristine 1 affected 2 skeletal remains not recorded
#>   Kingdom           0.0        0.0                0.0          0.0
#>   Phylum            7.5        9.0               24.9         25.7
#>   Class             4.6       15.0               32.6          4.1
#>   Order            19.6       13.6               10.7         11.0
#>   Family           14.6       21.6                7.8          1.1
#>   Genus             2.9        8.9                5.5          0.3
#>   Species          39.0       31.3                5.7          5.6
#>   Unresolved       11.8        0.7               12.7         52.2
n_stage <- tapply(diag$n_records, diag$digestion, sum)
n_stage
#>         0 pristine         1 affected 2 skeletal remains       not recorded 
#>                561               3494               2206               2269

Percentages are computed within each stage, so each stage adds up to 100% whatever its sample size. Always read them next to n_records: here the four columns hold 561, 3,494, 2,206, 2,269 records respectively.

Pooled, the share named to genus or species changes little between stage 0 (41.9%) and stage 1 (40.2%) and collapses at stage 2 (11.2%), while the share named only to a phylum or a class reaches 57.6%. Stage 0 has its own oddity: 11.8% of its records are unresolved, which a fresh prey should not be. These are unidentified material recorded as undigested, a reminder that the stage describes the record, not always the prey.

The “not recorded” column is not a fourth stage. 2,139 of its 2,269 records come from Denmark, and 52.2% of them are unresolved. A missing stage follows the data provider, and providers differ in how far they identify; dropping these records would not remove them at random.

Drawing it 

w_plot <- w[rowSums(w) > 0, ]            # no record stops at kingdom
cols <- c(grDevices::hcl.colors(nrow(w_plot) - 1, "Blues 3", rev = TRUE), "grey85")
barplot(w_plot, col = cols, xlim = c(0, 6.6), legend.text = TRUE,
        args.legend = list(x = "right", cex = 0.75, bty = "n"),
        names.arg = sub(" ", "\n", colnames(w_plot)),
        xlab = "Digestion stage", ylab = "% of records", cex.names = 0.75)

Predator by predator

Pooled profiles mix predators that eat different prey and were sampled by different countries. by = takes any column of the prepared data, including the predator:

top <- c("Atlantic cod", "Whiting", "European plaice", "Atlantic mackerel")
by_pred <- dv_digestion_diagnostic(prep, by = "predator_common")
by_pred <- by_pred[by_pred$by %in% top, ]
fine <- by_pred[by_pred$finest_rank %in% c("Genus", "Species"), ]
round(xtabs(p_records ~ by + digestion, data = fine), 1)   # % named to genus or species
#>                    digestion
#> by                  0 pristine 1 affected 2 skeletal remains not recorded
#>   Atlantic cod            73.0       63.7               21.1         21.0
#>   Atlantic mackerel        1.5        9.9                0.0          0.1
#>   European plaice         33.3       11.9                8.5          0.0
#>   Whiting                 29.9       32.6               10.8          9.9
xtabs(n_records ~ by + digestion, data = by_pred)          # records per cell
#>                    digestion
#> by                  0 pristine 1 affected 2 skeletal remains not recorded
#>   Atlantic cod             159       1237                393          515
#>   Atlantic mackerel         66        262                 73         1192
#>   European plaice            3        646               1003          238
#>   Whiting                  284        656                483          182
  • Atlantic cod shows the profile in its clearest form: the share named to genus or species falls from 73.0% at stage 0 to 63.7% at stage 1 and 21.1% at stage 2.
  • Whiting starts lower, at 29.9%, holds at stage 1 (32.6%) and drops at stage 2 (10.8%).
  • European plaice has only 3 records at stage 0, so its first column means nothing; at stages 1 and 2 it is 11.9% and 8.5%. Its three most frequent prey names, Ophiuroidea, Polychaeta, Bivalvia, are classes: much of what plaice eat is recorded at class whatever its stage.
  • Atlantic mackerel is almost never identified to genus or species, at any stage. Its four most frequent prey names are Unidentified material (817), Ammodytidae (318), Crustacea (243), Pisces (181): the limit here is how the prey were recorded, not how digested they were, and most of its records have no stage at all (1,192 of 1,593).

So the same stage does not mean the same identification depth in two predators, and a pooled profile can hide both a steep and a flat one.

How to read it

  • If the species share falls steeply with digestion, as for cod, fine-rank results rest mostly on fresh material. Consider reporting them for the freshest stages separately, with the sample size you lose by doing so.
  • Weight is affected twice: digested prey are both harder to name and lighter. A steep profile is a reason to be cautious with the weight currency in particular.
  • Use by = with other strata too, for example by = "country", when observers or protocols differ between them, or by = "year" when they changed over time.

The diagnostic describes identification; it does not correct for it. What digestion does to the diet estimate itself cannot be measured on real data, because the true diet is unknown. The vignette “A known diet” shows it on simulated data where the truth is known: how much a diet description moves when unidentified material is kept or dropped.

Reference

Buckland, A., Baker, R., Loneragan, N., & Sheaves, M. (2017). Standardising fish stomach content analysis: the importance of prey condition. Fisheries Research, 196, 126–140.
